chemistry: lithium-ion (HEV; prismatic NMC-type, not explicitly confirmed)
research_notes: Blue Energy Co., Ltd. is a JV between GS Yuasa (51%) and Honda (49%), founded 2009. The Osadano Plant sits within GS Yuasa's Osadano works at 1-37 Osadano-cho, Fukuchiyama City, Kyoto 620-0853. It manufactures lithium-ion CELLS for hybrid-electric vehicles (HEV); mass production began Feb 2011. A second building/expansion was added (~FY2022), raising capacity toward ~15 million HEV cells/year (per 2013 figures; unit-count, not GWh). No reliable annual GWh nameplate figure is published for this HEV cell site, so nameplate_capacity_gwh is left null (HEV cells are small; converting cell counts to GWh would be a guess). Chemistry/format: GS Yuasa HEV cells are prismatic lithium-ion (typically NMC-type) but not explicitly confirmed for this line - flagged accordingly. End market coded EV (automotive HEV traction/assist batteries). Coordinates left null - no precise source found. NOTE - distinct from the separate new Honda/GS Yuasa Blue Energy ~20 GWh EV cell plant announced April 2023 (¥434bn investment, operations from April 2027, mass production Oct 2027), which is a different (planned) facility and should be a separate row. Sources: Blue Energy corporate profile; GS Yuasa/Honda 2009 construction release; GS Yuasa 2020 second-plant release; Argus/electrive 2023 for the separate new plant.

AESC's flagship "mother factory" in the Ibaraki Central Industrial Complex Phase 2, Ibaraki-machi (茨城町), Higashiibaraki-gun, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. Address per AESC: 9-10 Chuo Kogyo Danchi, Ibaraki-machi. Manufactures battery CELLS (confirmed): fifth-generation "Gen5" liquid lithium-ion pouch cells, ternary/NMC chemistry, ~1.3x energy density vs Gen4. Construction of Building 1 started Oct 2021; completion ceremony Aug/Sep 2023; mass production began March 2024. Confirmed current annual nameplate 6 GWh (Building 1), ref year 2024 — enough for ~100,000 60kWh EVs. Supplies Nissan (new Leaf) and Honda (N-VAN e:). Announced Aug 2021 as a Nissan + Envision AESC joint investment (initial ¥50bn); AESC is now majority-owned by Envision Group (Nissan retained a minority stake). Expansion: a second building (further ~500bn yen investment reported Aug 2023) and a possible third building are planned to lift total nameplate to ~20 GWh/yr (earlier 2021 reports said 18 GWh). nameplate_capacity_gwh=20 reflects the eventual planned max; the 2024 confirmed operational figure of 6 GWh is captured in capacity_by_year_json. Exact ramp years for the 20 GWh target are not firmly dated, and 18 vs 20 GWh figures conflict across sources — hence moderate confidence. Coordinates not confirmed from a reliable source, left null (approx. area ~36.29N, 140.42E but not verified). Sources: AESC official (aesc-group.com), Nikkei xtech, TEPCO EV DAYS (evdays.tepco.co.jp, 2025-09-12), electrive/S&P Global, LNEWS.

Toshiba's Kashiwazaki Operations in Kashiwazaki Frontier Park, Kashiwazaki City, Niigata Prefecture, Japan is a dedicated SCiB rechargeable Li-ion battery cell manufacturing site. Chemistry is Toshiba's SCiB, which uses a lithium titanate (LTO) anode; both high-energy and high-power SCiB cells are made here and turned into modules/packs for automotive (EV), stationary (ESS) and industrial use, so end_market = mixed. Second SCiB facility announced 28 Oct 2009; plant opened 29 Sep 2010; SCiB cell/module volume production for EV applications began spring 2011. Initial ~25 billion yen investment, ~33,000 m2 floor area, initial capacity ~500,000 cells/month expected to exceed 1,000,000 cells/month in FY2011. In Dec 2018 Toshiba announced it would reinforce Kashiwazaki and build an additional SCiB plant at its Yokohama Complex (a separate site, not this one). No verified annual GWh/year nameplate figure could be sourced (public figures are in cells/month), so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null. Coordinates not confirmed from a reliable source, so lat/long left null. Sources: Toshiba press releases (2009 news release, 29 Sep 2010 Kashiwazaki opening release, 26 Dec 2018 battery business release); pv-magazine (18 Oct 2018).

plant_name: Honda GS Yuasa New Battery Plant (Blue Energy BEV lithium-ion plant)
research_notes: Joint project of Honda, GS Yuasa and their JV Blue Energy Co., Ltd. (Honda also formed Honda・GS Yuasa EV Battery R&D Co. in May 2023). Plans for mass production of high-capacity, high-power lithium-ion cells primarily for BEVs were approved by the Japanese government in May 2023. Total project cost ~¥434.1bn, with up to ~¥158.7bn in government subsidy. Annual nameplate capacity 20 GWh/year; plant to be commissioned April 2027, commercial production from October 2027, targeting full production by 2030 (capacity_ref_year set to 2030). Chemistry recorded as generic lithium-ion — sources say "high-capacity, high-power Li-ion for BEVs" but do not confirm a specific cathode (likely NMC, not verified); cell format not disclosed. Exact site not confirmed in English sources; likely at/near Blue Energy's existing Osadano Plant in Fukuchiyama, Kyoto Prefecture, so latitude/longitude left null. Status set to under_construction: GS Yuasa's Nov 2025 IR materials reference capex for the Blue Energy plant to reach production capacity ahead of the April 2027 commissioning, though the earliest 2023 releases framed it as "to build" (announced) — moderate confidence given some ambiguity vs. the separate HV-battery Blue Energy No.2 expansion. Corroborated by Argus, electrive, Yuasa/GS Yuasa releases and Nikkei/MarketScreener (~$3.21bn investment).

Murata's Yasu Plant (Yasu City, Shiga Prefecture, Japan) is a genuine battery CELL manufacturer, producing oxide-based ceramic all-solid-state batteries (surface-mount / SMD chip type) using Li-ion technology acquired from Sony combined with Murata's multilayer-ceramic-capacitor lamination know-how. Cells are very small (prototype capacity >10 mAh) and target wearables/IoT/consumer devices — explicitly NOT suited to EV or large-scale ESS. Mass production line capacity reported at ~100,000 units/month; because these are milliampere-hour-class micro cells, total annual output is negligible on a GWh scale, so nameplate_capacity_gwh is left null rather than invented (a 100k units/month, ~10 mAh line implies only on the order of a few tens of kWh/year, well below 0.001 GWh). Mass production began in fall 2021 (initial fiscal-2019 plan; commercial ramp confirmed 2021), hence status=operational, start_year=2021. Coordinates not confirmed from a source, left null. Chemistry recorded honestly as oxide-based all-solid-state. Sources: batteriesnews.com (Aug 2021), corroborated by Nikkei Asia and Murata official product news (murata.com/en-us/news/batteries/solid_state/2019/0626). Confidence moderate: site and technology well confirmed, but no GWh-scale figure exists and exact start date/coordinates are approximate.

Toshiba's second Japanese SCiB manufacturing facility, located at the TISS Yokohama complex in Isogo Ward, Yokohama, Kanagawa prefecture. Announced October 2018 with an investment of JPY 16.2 billion (~US$144m); three-storey building, ~27,000 sqm floor area; also serves as a production technology development centre. Construction began July 2019; production started October 2020, so status = operational. SCiB is a lithium-ion cell using a lithium titanate oxide (LTO) anode — genuine CELL manufacturing (not just pack/module), so is_cell_manufacturer = true. Toshiba's other SCiB cell site is at Kashiwazaki. The Yokohama plant was said to raise SCiB production capacity by >50% versus prior levels, but Toshiba has never disclosed an absolute output figure in GWh or cells/year for this site, so nameplate_capacity_gwh is left null. A further JPY 9.5 billion equipment investment at Yokohama was reported (Japanese trade press) with operations from ~April 2025, again without a stated GWh figure. End markets are mixed (EV/HEV, railway rolling stock, and stationary energy storage). Cell format mixed — Toshiba SCiB is offered in both prismatic and cylindrical formats. Coordinates left null as no source precisely confirmed the plant location. Capacity, precise coordinates unconfirmed → confidence 0.7.

jv_partners: GS Yuasa, Mitsubishi Corporation, Mitsubishi Motors
research_notes: Lithium Energy Japan (LEJ) is a JV between GS Yuasa (parent/operator), Mitsubishi Corporation and Mitsubishi Motors, established 2007. The Kusatsu City (Shiga Prefecture) plant was the world's first mass-production site for large automotive lithium-ion cells, using the LEV50 50Ah large prismatic cell for the Mitsubishi i-MiEV EV. Line 1 started shipping June 2009 at ~200,000 cells/yr; Line 2 came online June 2010 adding ~400,000 cells/yr for a Kusatsu total of ~600,000 cells/yr (sources: gs-yuasa.com press releases, Green Car Congress). Larger-volume production later moved to LEJ's separate Ritto plant (~0.8 GWh, ~4.4 million cells/yr) — that is a different physical site and is NOT included in this Kusatsu row. nameplate_capacity_gwh (~0.11 GWh/yr) is DERIVED, not directly sourced: 600,000 cells x 50Ah x ~3.7V nominal ~= 111 MWh; the 2009 figure (~0.037 GWh) is 200,000 cells similarly derived. These GWh values are my own calculation from sourced cell counts and the sourced LEV50 spec, hence lowered confidence. Chemistry: LEV50 is a manganese-based lithium-ion cell (lithium manganese oxide / NMC-type). Status: recorded operational as the LEJ Kusatsu site (GS Yuasa's lithium operations continue), but current 2024-2026 operating status and capacity were not confirmed by a recent source — i-MiEV production wound down around 2021, so present output may be reduced or repurposed. Coordinates left null (specific plant site not sourced). Most detailed capacity figures date from 2009-2012.

chemistry: mixed: sulfide-based all-solid-state, plus lithium/alkaline primary (coin) cells
research_notes:
Ono Works (小野事業所) is a Maxell battery cell manufacturing site at 5 Takumidai, Ono City, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan (675-1322), in the Ono industrial park. It is the operating company Maxell, Ltd.'s energy-business hub; ultimate listed parent is Maxell Holdings, Ltd.

CELL MANUFACTURER: yes. The site manufactures battery cells — it is Maxell's technical and production hub for small all-solid-state batteries and also produces primary/micro (coin) batteries (tens of millions of units/month cited). Maxell began mass production of the world's first small sulfide-based all-solid-state battery (coin type) in June 2023 at this site, hence start_year=2023 for solid-state (the site itself has produced batteries for decades). It later developed a cylindrical all-solid-state cell (PSB23280) and targets a medium-sized cell around end of FY2027; solid-state business sales target ~30bn yen by FY2030. In Nov 2024 Maxell announced ~5bn yen for a new primary-battery line at Ono Works for medical-device demand.

STATUS: operational (mass production ongoing). Note: Maxell announced in 2025 it is ending prismatic lithium-ion battery production, but primary batteries and all-solid-state cell production at Ono Works continue.

CAPACITY: no meaningful annual GWh nameplate is published — output is small-format/coin and micro cells measured in units/month, not GWh — so nameplate_capacity_gwh is left null (per no-guessing rule). 

COORDINATES: street address confirmed (兵庫県小野市匠台5) but precise lat/long not from an authoritative source, so left null rather than guessed.

Chemistry/format/end-market are 'mixed': sulfide all-solid-state coin + cylindrical cells and lithium/alkaline primary coin cells, serving medical devices, industrial/IoT, sensors and wearables. Confidence moderate (0.68): plant existence, cell-manufacturing role and operational status well sourced; capacity/coordinates unquantified.

Sources: Maxell/BusinessWire all-solid-state release (2024-10-04); Maxell EU/USA solid-state mass-production releases (2023); Maxell corporate location page and automation-news.jp (2024-11) primary-battery line at Ono Works.

Eliiy Power Co., Ltd. is a Japanese manufacturer of large-format prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells aimed at stationary energy storage (ESS) rather than EVs. The Kawasaki site (Kawasaki-ku, Kawasaki City, Kanagawa) is its cell-manufacturing base. Two plants on the site: Kawasaki Plant No.1 completed April 2010 with ~200,000 cells/year (mass production began 2010); Kawasaki Plant No.2 completed June 2012 with ~1,000,000 cells/year, a highly automated, cleanroom-grade line. Reported expansion toward ~1.5 million cells/year following a 2015 supply deal with Enphase Energy. A 2024 Nikkei feature describes the Kawasaki plant as fully automated (materials mixing through assembly, inspection and packing), ~29,000 m2, ~200 workers. Site remains operational. Capacity is reported in cells/year, not GWh; a firm per-cell spec was not sourced, so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null rather than guessed (order of magnitude is sub-1 GWh/year given ~1-1.5 million large prismatic cells). Coordinates not sourced. Cathode = lithium iron phosphate (confirmed by company technology page via search). Confidence moderate: consistent multi-source news/Wikipedia coverage, but capacity in GWh and exact current status year unconfirmed. Some primary company/news pages (eliiypower.co.jp, bestmag, greencarcongress) returned 403/unreachable during research.

FDK's Washizu Plant is at 614 Washizu, Kosai-shi, Shizuoka 431-0431, Japan — the site where FDK originated. It manufactures primary battery CELLS: alkaline batteries (operated under subsidiary FDK Energy Co., Ltd.) and historically primary lithium batteries. In 2022 FDK consolidated high-capacity cylindrical primary lithium battery production to its Tottori plant, leaving Washizu focused on alkaline battery manufacturing. So it is a genuine cell manufacturer, but of PRIMARY (non-rechargeable) consumer/industrial cells, not a Li-ion/EV/ESS gigafactory. Note: FDK's all-solid-state SMD battery mass production is at the separate Kosai Plant (also in Kosai city), NOT Washizu. No GWh/year nameplate exists for this plant — primary alkaline/lithium output is measured in units, not GWh, so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null. Precise plant coordinates not sourced (approx Kosai/Washizu area ~34.71N, 137.53E) so left null to avoid guessing. Confidence moderate: product mix and location well sourced from FDK corporate pages, but no annual capacity figure and this is arguably out of scope for a lithium-ion gigafactory database. Sources: FDK Washizu plant page (fdk.com/company_e/div_washizu-e.html); FDK 2022-03-01 lithium battery consolidation release; FDK Corporation Wikipedia.

plant_name: APB Fukui Center Takefu Factory (Echizen Plant)
chemistry: all-polymer lithium-ion (LFP cathode, resin-coated bipolar electrode)
research_notes:
APB's first ("1st") all-polymer battery plant, formally the APB Fukui Center Takefu Factory, in Echizen City, Fukui, Japan (address given in local press as Shoden-cho, Echizen City). Site area ~32,800 m2, floor area ~9,600 m2. Construction/acquisition 2020; opened 2021 with full "mass-production verification" from October 2021. This is a genuine cell manufacturer: it produces all-polymer battery cells, a next-generation lithium-ion design using resin-coated (gel-polymer) bipolar electrodes and an LFP cathode, targeted first at stationary storage (ESS) for buildings and renewable energy. Cell format recorded as pouch as the closest match — the true structure is a bipolar resin laminate, not a conventional wound/prismatic cell.

Capacity is uncertain and conflicting across sources. The Takefu line was to start at ~200 MWh/yr (0.2 GWh, captured in capacity_by_year_json for 2021) and expand to ~3 GWh/yr "within several years" via added equipment — recorded as the eventual nameplate, though never achieved. A separate, larger 8 GWh Japanese plant was planned for ~2026 but is a different (never-built) site, not this one; an earlier "1 GWh by 2023" target also appeared. Treat the 3 GWh nameplate as a plan, hence lower confidence.

Status: the plant did reach production (hence "operational"), but APB collapsed — funding withdrawn late 2024, all staff given retirement notices Feb 2025, and the Fukui District Court issued a bankruptcy order on 23 April 2025 (total debts ~JPY 3.485bn). The site is effectively defunct/idle as of 2026; no schema enum captures "closed". Parent listed as Sanyo Chemical Industries (largest shareholder / consolidating investor); APB also had many investors (Nissan licensed core IP, plus Obayashi, Toyota Tsusho, Yokogawa) but it is not a formal JV. Coordinates left null — not confirmed from a source. Primary source is the Sanyo Chemical English release on the 1st plant; capacity/expansion and bankruptcy details cross-checked against Japanese trade press (Nikkei, Chunichi, smarthouse-readers, TDB) and Digitimes; accessed 2026-07-18.

chemistry: solid-state (sulfide-based all-solid-state; part of line dedicated to lithium metal)
research_notes: R&D/pilot line at SK On's Future Technology Institute (research center) in Daejeon, South Korea. Completion ceremony held mid-September 2025 (reported 15-16 Sep 2025); the ~4,628 sq m pilot plant produces prototype cells for client evaluation and R&D, not commercial-volume output. Focus is sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries, with part of the line dedicated to solid-state lithium metal batteries. Uses SK On's proprietary "WIP-free" (no warm isostatic press) manufacturing process; partner Solid Power supplied/finalised equipment. As of Nov 2025 the line was set to begin operation before end of 2025, so as of mid-2026 it is treated as operational. Commercialization of ASSBs targeted for 2029 (accelerated from 2030), with energy density target of 800 Wh/L medium-term and 1,000 Wh/L long-term. No annual GWh nameplate capacity is disclosed for this pilot line, so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null. It manufactures actual cells (prototypes), hence is_cell_manufacturer=true. Coordinates not confirmed by a source, left null. Corroborating sources: Korea Herald (koreaherald.com/article/10576661), electrive.com (2025/09/16), electrek.co (2025/09/16), Korea Herald exclusive on pilot output start (koreaherald.com/article/10617647, Nov 2025).

chemistry: perovskite (solar PV — not an electrochemical storage battery)
research_notes: MISCLASSIFICATION — this is NOT a battery cell plant. The "Ritto film battery pilot line" is Sekisui Chemical's Shiga Ritto plant (滋賀栗東工場) in Ritto, Shiga Prefecture, where the company develops/pilots its film-type PEROVSKITE SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic). In Japanese, "太陽電池" (solar cell) contains the character 電池 (battery/cell), which is the likely source of the "film battery" label — but it is a solar PV cell, not an electrochemical energy storage or EV battery cell. Sekisui uses a 30cm-wide roll-to-roll process at pilot scale; the commercial 100 MW production line (announced Dec 2024, targeting April 2027) is being built at a former Sharp factory in Sakai, Osaka — a separate site, and measured in MW of PV, not GWh of storage. Separately, Sekisui did develop a film-type lithium-ion battery (2013 R&D, 2016 commercial), but that work was associated with Tsukuba/ENAX, not the Ritto site. is_cell_manufacturer set false; capacity/format/end_market left null as they do not apply to a PV pilot line. Recommend excluding from the battery gigafactory database.

"S-Line" is Samsung SDI's all-solid-state battery (ASB) pilot line at its R&D Center in Suwon, Gyeonggi Province, South Korea. The name S stands for solid, sole and Samsung SDI. Construction began March 2022; it is a 6,500 sq m R&D pilot line — the first dedicated solid-state pilot line built by a Korean battery maker. It began producing prototype/sample cells in 2023 and has supplied samples to customers; in Oct 2025 Samsung SDI began a real-world validation project with BMW (using Solid Power cells alongside). Chemistry is a proprietary sulfide solid electrolyte with an anode-less (silver-carbon) design, energy density ~900 Wh/L, prismatic format, targeting super-premium EV mass production in 2027. This is a lab/pilot-scale line, NOT a commercial gigafactory — no GWh/year nameplate capacity has been disclosed, so nameplate_capacity_gwh is left null. Coordinates left null (not source-confirmed to the exact site). Status "operational" reflects the pilot line running and producing sample cells; commercial mass production is separately planned at other Samsung SDI sites by 2027. Sources: KED Global (2022-03-15), Samsung SDI newsroom, InsideEVs, Korea JoongAng Daily (2025).

Sella 2 is a lithium-ion NMC pouch battery CELL manufacturing plant in Eumseong Innovation City, Chungcheongbuk-do, South Korea, built by SolarEdge using Kokam technology. Construction began 2020, plant opened/completed May 2022 with test production, mass production ramping in H2 2022. Nameplate ~2 GWh/year (SolarEdge's first GWh-scale cell fab). Cells intended for ESS, UPS and mobile applications (mixed end market). Kokam is a subsidiary of SolarEdge (majority stake acquired 2018-2019), NOT a joint venture, so jv_partners left null. IMPORTANT: On 27 Nov 2024 SolarEdge announced closure of its (utility-scale) energy storage division and is shuttering Sella 2 ahead of an asset sale, with ~500 layoffs (mostly South Korea) completing in H1 2025. Status recorded as 'operational' as the historical/closest-fit enum value since the plant was built and ran 2022-2024, but it is being wound down/sold as of 2025 (schema has no 'closed' status). Precise site coordinates not confirmed by a source, so latitude/longitude left null. Sources: energy-storage.news (2022-05-26 opening; 2024-11 closure), SolarEdge investor releases, pv-magazine, Green Car Congress, InvestKorea.

Siheung is Kokam's original/legacy headquarters and battery cell manufacturing site, located at Jeongwang-dong, Siheung-si, Gyeonggi-do, South Korea. Kokam (founded 1989, entered Li-polymer battery manufacturing late 1990s) develops and manufactures lithium-ion/lithium-polymer secondary cells in pouch (lithium-polymer) format, chemistry predominantly NMC. Serves mixed end markets: ESS/BESS, e-mobility, marine, defence and UPS. Kokam was acquired by Israel's SolarEdge Technologies in 2018 (deal closed 2019), so parent company is SolarEdge. IMPORTANT DISAMBIGUATION: This Siheung site is DISTINCT from the newer, larger 'Sella 2' plant (2 GWh/yr, NMC pouch cells) in Eumseong Innovation City, Chungcheongbuk-do, which opened/ramped in 2022. Kokam has also historically operated a ~150 MWh/yr plant in Nonsan, Chungnam. A clean, current nameplate GWh/yr figure for the SIHEUNG site specifically could not be confirmed from a reputable source (company legacy capacity was sub-GWh, historically a few hundred MWh scale), so nameplate_capacity_gwh, capacity_ref_year and coordinates are left null rather than guessed. Status set operational as it is a long-running facility, though ongoing production levels at the legacy Siheung site (vs. consolidation into Sella 2) are not independently confirmed for 2026. Confidence held at 0.5 due to unconfirmed capacity and current operating status. Corroborating context: SolarEdge/Kokam Sella 2 coverage (pv-magazine, energy-storage.news, Green Car Congress, SolarEdge IR, 2022) and Kokam company profiles listing the Siheung/Jeongwang-dong address.

Enertech International Co., Ltd. (est. 2001) is a specialist lithium-ion secondary battery maker headquartered in Chungju (Yongtan-dong), Chungcheongbuk-do, South Korea. It manufactures high-performance pouch-type Li-ion cells (adopting domestic high-nickel NMC cathode materials, per 2021 ETNews reporting) plus modules and packs, for both EV and ESS markets — confirming this is a genuine cell-manufacturing site (is_cell_manufacturer=true), operational. Status high-confidence; capacity NOT confidently sourced. The frequently quoted "300 GWh by 2030" is an aspirational corporate vision from the CEO, NOT a plant nameplate, so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null. In Jan 2023 the company signed a KRW 35bn (2023–2024) investment agreement with Chungcheongbuk-do/Chungju to expand secondary-battery module/pack lines, reportedly aiming to more than triple output — figures not given in GWh. Russia's Rosatom (via subsidiary Renera) acquired ~49% of Enertech; note a separate planned cell facility in Russia (~2GWh, from 2025) is a DIFFERENT site and excluded here. Coordinates left null (approx Chungju city area but exact plant coordinates unconfirmed). start_year=2001 reflects company/plant founding. Sources: energy-storage.news (Rosatom stake, ESS/cell maker), enertechint.com company profile, ETNews (high-nickel pouch cells), Chungju investment MOU reporting.

Kumyang (금양), a former foaming-agent maker pivoting into cylindrical Li-ion cells, is building the "Gijang Dream Factory" in Gijang-gun, northern Busan (site ~180,296 sqm). MOU with Busan Jan 2023; groundbreaking Sep 2023. It manufactures battery cells (not just packs): planned nameplate of 3.7 GWh of 21700 cells (2 lines, ~200m units/yr) plus ~12.6 GWh of 4695 cells (~100m units/yr) = 16.3 GWh total at full nameplate. Chemistry is NCM (nickel-based, "46-series NCM lithium"); format cylindrical (21700 and Kumyang's flagship 4695, which it claims as a world-first). STATUS: under construction — reported 73% complete Nov 2024 and ~85% complete Feb 2026, with repeated delays. Latest plan (early 2026): finish building ~Nov 2025, 21700 line normal operation from Jan 2026 (3.7 GWh), 4695 equipment install by end-Jun 2026 and mass production from Jul 2026 (adds ~12.6 GWh). capacity_by_year_json reflects this planned ramp and is indicative given slippage risk. Offtake/tech links: licensed StoreDot XFC fast-charge tech (Mar 2025) for EV cells; large supply deal cited with US-based Nanotech Energy. RISK: Kumyang is under a delisting-review improvement period (to ~Apr 2026) after a disclaimer of audit opinion on 2024 results and severe funding strain — completion timeline is uncertain. Coordinates not confirmed from a source, left null. Capacity split figure appears as 12.5–12.6 GWh across sources; used 12.6. Sources: Korea Herald (koreaherald.com/article/3848365); MarkLines news 293722 & 304270; Busan Ilbo (busan.com, Oct 2024 & Feb 2026); efactorynews; Kumyang IR (kyc.co.kr).

EIG (Energy Innovation Group Ltd.) is a South Korean manufacturer of large-format pouch lithium-ion battery cells, with headquarters and manufacturing plant in Cheonan, South Korea. Confirmed cell maker (not just pack assembly): produces pouch NMC cells such as the 20 Ah C020, plus LTO cells for 12V/48V stop-start micro-hybrid, telecom and military markets, and grid/stationary ESS (ePLB cell/pack/BMS product line). Chemistry: primarily NMC pouch, also LTO. End market: mixed (EV/micro-hybrid, ESS, telecom, military). This is a small, legacy, sub-gigafactory-scale producer — no reliable annual GWh nameplate capacity figure could be sourced, so nameplate_capacity_gwh left null. STATUS UNCERTAIN: several supplier-directory sources (e.g. Komachine) indicate EIG has ceased operations / closed down; status recorded as 'operational' to reflect its historical production but with low confidence given closure signals. Note: a separate/related entity 'EGI Battery' announced a new lithium-ion plant in Michigan, USA in 2025 — not confirmed to be the same Cheonan site. Exact plant coordinates and founding/start year not confirmed by a source, left null. Primary source: Komachine supplier profile (HTTP 403 on direct fetch; details corroborated via web-search snippets and eePower/OpenEI references).

chemistry: lithium primary (Li/SOCl2, Li/MnO2); also thermal batteries and lithium-ion capacitors
research_notes: Could not confirm the existence of any Vitzrocell plant in Nonsan. Vitzrocell (KRX:082920) is a lithium PRIMARY battery cell manufacturer (Li/SOCl2, Li/MnO2 bobbin/wound cells, thermal/ampoule batteries, super/hybrid capacitors) - not a Li-ion "gigafactory". All confirmed manufacturing is in Dangjin-si, Chungcheongnam-do (70 Induspark-ro, Hapdeok-eup) - a smart campus rebuilt after the April 2017 fire that destroyed its earlier Yesan-gun plant. No source (company site, KRX filings, Korean trade press, D&B/Bloomberg profiles) references a Nonsan site under Vitzrocell; Nonsan battery firms are other companies (e.g. Routejade; Enovix's ex-SolarEdge Li-ion line). This "Nonsan Plant / Vitzrocell" candidate is almost certainly a mis-attribution. As a primary-battery maker, capacity is not measured in GWh/year and is negligible in electrotech terms; all quantitative fields left null. is_cell_manufacturer set false because the specific Nonsan site cannot be confirmed to exist (the company itself does make cells, but not large-format Li-ion). Recommend dropping this row or reassigning to Vitzrocell's Dangjin campus if the intent was Vitzrocell's cell plant.

LiBEST Inc. is a KAIST spin-off (founded 2016) headquartered at 193 Munji-ro, Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. It manufactures flexible lithium-ion (Li-polymer) battery CELLS for wearables (smartwatches, smart rings, vital patches, AR glasses), so it is a genuine cell manufacturer, not pack assembly. Its first factory — a "one-stop" R&D-to-mass-production plant in the Daejeon Dungok International Business Belt (total land ~1,260 pyeong, floor area ~867 pyeong, six process rooms) — held its completion ceremony on 8 August 2023, with mass production targeted for Q4 2023. Reported output is measured in UNITS, not GWh: ~25,000 flexible cells/month at completion, targeting 100,000/month by end-2023 and 200,000/month in 2024. These are tiny wearable pouch cells (sub-Wh each), so annual output is on the order of a fraction of an MWh — well below 0.001 GWh — and no GWh nameplate figure is published; nameplate_capacity_gwh and capacity_by_year_json left null rather than converting unit counts into a fabricated GWh figure. Status = operational (factory completed, mass production underway). Coordinates left null: the HQ address (Munji-ro, near KAIST) may differ from the Dungok Business Belt plant site and no precise plant coordinate was confirmed. The candidate label "pilot" is somewhat misleading — LiBEST describes this as its first mass-production factory. research_notes: Battery CELL manufacturing plant in Windsor, Ontario (1 NextStar Way, off E.C. Row Expressway / Banwell Road), Canada's first large-scale/commercial battery cell factory. 50:50 JV between LG Energy Solution and Stellantis; combined investment over CAD 5 billion (~USD 4.1bn), backed by Canadian federal/provincial subsidies. Timeline: JV announced March 2022; construction paused mid-2023 over subsidy dispute, resumed after July 2023 deal; battery module/pack production started Oct 2024 (using cells shipped in initially); on-site lithium-ion CELL production began late Nov 2025, reached 1 million cells Feb 2026; grand opening held 5 March 2026 = now operational. Nameplate capacity 49.5 GWh/yr (upgraded from original 45 GWh), enough for ~450,000 EVs/yr. Chemistry: originally NMC pouch cells for Stellantis EVs; in Nov 2025 the plant announced adding an LFP line for stationary/BESS energy storage (commercial ESS production targeted Dec 2025) to adapt to softer EV demand, so end market is now mixed (EV + ESS). Cell format recorded as pouch (LGES standard for NMC); LFP-line format not separately confirmed — moderate confidence on cell_format. Coordinates left null (approx Windsor site ~42.28N, 82.92W but no sourced precise coordinate). Sources: NextStar/Stellantis press releases, electrive (2026-03-06), ess-news (2025-11-11), electricautonomy (2024-10-23).

Northvolt Six was a fully-integrated lithium-ion gigafactory announced September 2023, sited between Saint-Basile-le-Grand and McMasterville in Quebec's Monteregie region (~30 km east of Montreal). Planned annual cell-manufacturing nameplate of 60 GWh at full build-out, with an initial 30 GWh phase 1, alongside adjacent cathode active material production and battery recycling. Chemistry/format taken from Northvolt's standard NMC prismatic cells; not separately confirmed for this specific site, hence flagged as planned. Total investment ~USD 5bn (CAD 7bn); first production originally targeted for 2026.

STATUS: The project effectively collapsed. Northvolt's Swedish parent filed for bankruptcy in March 2025. Site preparation/land clearing had begun in 2024 (hence 'under_construction' as the furthest state reached), but the cell plant was never built or operated. In August 2025 US battery startup Lyten expressed interest in acquiring the Quebec site (after buying Northvolt's Swedish/German assets), but talks stalled over funding demands. Quebec's government ended all Northvolt financing in September 2025, having lost a ~CAD 270m equity investment and recovered ~CAD 200m from frozen North American subsidiary accounts; the province declared the partnership a failure. As of this research date the plant is not operational and its future is highly uncertain. The enum lacks a 'cancelled'/'abandoned' option; 'under_construction' reflects the peak state reached, but the project should be treated as stalled/dead. Coordinates are town-level for Saint-Basile-le-Grand, not a surveyed plant location, so treat as approximate.

Sources: Northvolt announcement (northvolt.com/manufacturing/six/), electrive.com (2025-09-12), Globe and Mail, BNN Bloomberg (2025-09-02/05), Global News, ESG Today (Lyten).

Announced 25 April 2024 as part of Honda's ~C$15bn (US$11bn) comprehensive EV value chain in Ontario. This is a stand-alone Honda EV battery (cell) plant in Alliston, Ontario, sited alongside Honda's existing Alliston vehicle plant and a planned new EV assembly plant. Confirmed cell manufacturer: nameplate 36 GWh/year "once fully operational"; EV production was slated to begin in 2028. The broader value chain also included a CAM/pCAM plant (JV with POSCO Future M) and a separator plant (JV with Asahi Kasei), but those are separate material plants, not this cell site — the cell/battery plant itself was described as stand-alone Honda (no JV partner recorded here). Chemistry and cell format not disclosed in the announcement (left null). STATUS CAVEAT: Honda paused the project for two years in 2025, then in May 2026 (reported ~5-14 May 2026) moved to an "indefinite suspension"/shelving of the Alliston EV and battery complex amid weak US EV demand and a pivot to hybrids. Construction never began, so status recorded as "announced" rather than under_construction; the project is currently indefinitely suspended and may not proceed. No confirmed plant coordinates found, so latitude/longitude left null (Alliston town is ~44.15N, -79.87W but exact battery-plant plot unconfirmed). Suspension sourced via Global News (globalnews.ca/news/11849146) and Electrek (electrek.co/2026/05/05), May 2026.
